rows.design:
Use: a town-garden fruit-training workshop with sheltered outdoor work bays. This is a workshop plus architectural garden enclosure, not a claimed historic orchard. No plant growth, harvest, climate effect or global vegetation-density change is introduced.

Volume and roof: a substantial enclosed gabled brick tool/work lodge joins one end of a tall, thick serpentine brick wall. The wall creates alternating genuinely concave OUTDOOR work bays, with real grounded masonry, inner/outer faces and coping. One selected bay has a low simple planar lean-to weather roof carried between the wall and substantial outer posts; the other stays open to the sky. The enclosed lodge must remain a full usable building, not a token tiny shed; the serpentine wall must remain an equally substantial spatial enclosure, not a low decorative fence. Avoid a continuous S-shaped floor-and-roof envelope.

Entrance and openings: the lodge has one ordinary ground door, a broad small-paned work window and a side loading door. Outdoor bays are entered through their open mouths. Optional static trellis rails are secondary; the design must remain distinctive with plants, signs and props removed. No invented indoor room is claimed inside the free-standing wall.

Closest existing structures: withebasket v748 is an enclosed continuous S-plan workshop with a matching continuous S ridge and glazed convex bays; cloverseed v624 is a U-shaped group of open timber stalls plus store; ashfives v736 is a single three-wall roofless court; elmstone v700 is one four-pier open shed with a rear tool strip. The existing garden-life props include small potting/croquet/orchard-press settings, not this tall load-bearing serpentine enclosure/workshop compound.

Concrete difference: a closed gabled lodge plus a free-standing thick curved wall organising two-sided outdoor bays, with only selective low shelter. Its solid/void distribution is the inverse of the enclosed S ribbon. Its roof system is finite and conventional: one gable plus one simple clipped lean-to, no new ambiguous valley or saddle.

Reject if: it becomes Withebasket with windows omitted; wall thickness or coping is painted; both bays are enclosed or covered by a common roof; the wall is only a small garden fence around a generic shed; or vegetation/colour supplies the only identity. The compound is a deliberate architectural-enclosure entry, not a promise of a conventional all-enclosed house.

Shape key: substantial-gabled-workshop-terminal-tall-serpentine-brick-wall-real-opposed-open-work-bays-one-planar-lean-to.

rows.design:
Use: a small-town craft-pattern exhibition gallery. The title is fictional and gives no claim of a named historical building, flood protection, a new market economy or public-access routing.

Volume and roof: four substantial enclosed upper gallery ranges form one continuous square ring around a LARGE true sky-open central court. The ENTIRE ground tier beneath ALL four ranges is open between a restrained number of spaced grounded masonry piers. There are no ground-floor anchor rooms, perimeter back walls or central support block. A continuous annular floor carries the upper rooms; its underside and the space beneath must be real visible geometry. The upper ranges are occupied-depth rooms with inner and outer walls, not a thin rail or rooftop walkway. Use a simple continuous flat lead roof with low inner and outer parapets over the square annulus. The central roof opening aligns with the court and stays open to the sky. Finite rectangular roof strips and resolved corner joins are preferable to introducing new ambiguous valleys for novelty.

Entrance and openings: a single substantial exterior stair terminates at an actual upper landing and recessed gallery door. Upper walls have rhythmically spaced modest sash/work windows on outside and courtyard faces. Ground access is the open perimeter between the piers; no false gate arch is painted on a filled base. The staircase occupies one limited edge only and must not fill a whole side of the undercroft. No props or signs supply the identity.

Closest existing structures: piecehall v256 has four tall grounded range volumes with inner attached gallery orders and a separate lower eastern arcade; its main range volumes start at ground, not above a fully open tier. Globe v428 has continuous grounded outer polygonal walls around its theatre yard. Faversham v276 is one solid raised hall without a central court. Fennelhoney v732 is a grounded low polygonal ring with an open court and an inward-sloping roof. Hollyrecords v668 has a grounded square reading ring and high diamond core with four lightwells, not one wholly open central court. Older college()/cloister() in british-college-manor-art014.js combines tall grounded ranges and separate low open cloisters; quadrangleMarket() in british-use-scales-hospitality021.js has grounded front/rear rooms and one-storey side arcades with solid outer backs.

Concrete difference: a complete occupied room-ring is raised above an entirely open four-sided ground tier, leaving both a vertical sky court and horizontal ground-level sightlines under every range. The support topology, upper circulation ring and court relationship must distinguish the whole structure. It is neither a solid raised hall with an ornamental roof hole nor a conventional grounded court whose facade has arcade trim.

Reject if: any upper range drops to form a ground anchor room, the central court is roofed or filled, pier spacing closes into a wall, the court shrinks to a token skylight, the upper ring is only a skinny balcony, or a dark ground texture fakes the undercroft. A valid native set must show both court opening and meaningful ground-tier transparency without labels. The simple flat roof is not itself claimed as the novel feature.

rows.design:
Use: a static hop-drying and sorting-house exhibit; no production chain or claim to reproduce a named oast.

Volume and roof: one substantial cylindrical brick drying kiln carries a tall uninterrupted conical tiled/slate roof. It joins directly and off-axis into the rear-side wall of a long, two-storey rectangular sorting/store range with a complete gable. The kiln and range are co-dominant masses: neither a tiny cone stuck on a warehouse nor a central rotunda with small appendages. The junction is asymmetric and has a finite shared chord/opening: literal geometric tangency would create a zero-width connection and is not allowed. Resolve the wall/roof junction without a thin air gap or coplanar flicker, and keep the cone's eave above the adjoining range roof where necessary. There is no glass bridge between the two.

Entrance and openings: the store has a broad recessed loading entrance and a modest end stair/upper loading door; paired small work windows occupy its long sides. The kiln has sparse narrow lower lights and an ordinary maintenance door. A small cowl may be secondary static detail, but its omission must not erase the identity. This document makes no operating kiln/fire-safety claim.

Closest existing structures: sissinghurst v304 is an array of eight square pyramidal oasts; celandinewire v676 is two separated unequal drums joined by glazing; dittanygeology v868 is one central cone with two opposed low straight wings; gladstone v296 has several bulbous bottle hovels and a court.

Concrete difference: one straight-sided round kiln under a straight-sided cone, joined off-centre to one tall long house, with the side junction and loading elevation integral to the silhouette. It has no bottle neck, second drum, opposed wing axis or repeated kiln battery.

Reject if: only the cowl differentiates it, the cylinder is shrunk to a turret, the storage range becomes a low Dittany wing, or a gap/glass link turns it into Celandine.

Shape key: one-tall-cylindrical-conical-kiln-off-axis-finite-chord-joined-long-two-storey-gabled-sorting-range.

rows.design:
Use: an original static post-mill exhibit; no wind, animation, power or milling simulation.

Volume and roof: a compact oblong timber mill cabin with a steep complete gable stands high above an exposed single central structural post and broad diagonal trestle. The support consists of actual grounded crossed timbers/braces, with substantial open air beneath and around the cabin. Add a real rear tail porch and inclined access stair terminating at its door. The whole cabin is carried by the central support system; there is no masonry tower shell or filled ground-storey skirt.

Entrance and openings: a small rear door at the porch, one wider side work window and narrow end lights. Static lattice sails can be present on the opposite face but are secondary: the central-post/trestle/box-house/tail-access arrangement must remain visibly distinct with sails hidden. Keep every extremity inside the native sprite and plot envelope.

Closest existing structures: cley v280 is a tapered multi-storey masonry tower with balcony and sails; burnham v324 is a tall square room over many vertical piles; hartcurrier v784 is a broad loft over a full masonry spine with two side undercrofts.

Concrete difference: a discrete gabled timber machine-house is carried by one exposed central post and diagonal trestle, with a long rear access tail. Both the support topology and whole-body proportion differ from the tower, pile platform and spine-supported loft.

Reject if: trestles are hairline trim lost at native scale, a hidden opaque pedestal fills the underside, the house becomes a tall tower, or sails alone carry the identity. Prioritise native visibility of the central post, grounded diagonal feet and true empty underbody.

Shape key: oblong-gabled-timber-mill-cabin-single-exposed-central-post-diagonal-trestle-open-underbody-tail-stair.

rows.design:
Use: an outdoor recital shelter, with no sound or crowd mechanic.

Volume and roof: a thick hemispherical roof is cut vertically at its diameter to form a genuine open half-dome. Its curved rear enclosure and two substantial masonry side cheeks surround a deep walk-in cavity. The front is a full-width arch, not a window wall, colonnade or dark painted end. A low rectangular stage projects a little beyond the mouth. The roof must curve in both horizontal principal directions; a half-cylinder or tapering conoid is not equivalent.

Entrance and openings: the open mouth is the access. A small door in one rear-side wall may serve storage, but no separate large annex should compete with the shell. There is no need for decorative musical symbols. The inner soffit and side thickness remain visible; all top/back surfaces close properly without filling the front cavity.

Closest existing structures: eastbourne v408 already has a curved rear stage wall and four perimeter stage columns beneath a shallow saucer; its flanking colonnades use straight rectangular decks; shellwickpetitions v828 is an enclosed D-plan room under a radial planar half-hip; wrenumbrella v764 is a closed conoid hall; myrtlewireless v876 is a long closed semicylindrical shell. The older seasideConcertHall007 in british-publiclife-art.js has a separate closed entrance volume under a complete opaque ribbed dome, not a half-dome with an exposed walk-in cavity.

Concrete difference: an exposed deep concave interior beneath a two-directionally curved half-dome, with a broad genuinely open arch mouth and projecting stage. This is not merely one of those closed halls with an unlit front.

Reject if: the mouth is glazed or backed by an opaque wall, roof curvature is constant along its depth, the half-dome is replaced by an independent shallow saucer on perimeter stage columns like Eastbourne, or a dark disc is used to fake the hollow. Check the cut rim and the rear volume in all rotations.

Shape key: true-open-front-half-dome-recital-shell-curved-rear-enclosure-thick-arched-rim-low-projecting-stage.

rows.design:
Use: a bank-entry barn and rural storage exhibit; no storage capacity or terrain simulation.

Volume and roof: one broad rectangular gabled upper barn has genuinely different front and rear ground-access levels. A substantial model-owned earth bank meets the rear upper-floor doorway. At the opposite front, the lower level is exposed as a deep open masonry arcade below the enclosed timber upper barn. The bank is part of the asset, with its own closed side retaining cheeks and sloped faces; it must not edit map terrain. Use a low enough floor rise and long enough bank approach to fit the plot without a token near-vertical dirt wedge.

Entrance and openings: a large upper rear loading door is reached directly from the bank, while the front lower arcade has real depth and visible supports. Side elevations show the floor/bank relationship. Legacy coxwell v108 is a fully grounded closed stone barn with cross porch and buttresses; it has neither this upper rear bank entry nor an exposed lower front arcade. The upper long walls have small high ventilation/work windows and the gable end a plain loft opening. Roof: one complete ordinary gable, without a tower or extra ornamental roof.

Closest existing structures: cressice v716 is an earth-covered low vault with a small receiving room; faversham v276 is a wholly raised council hall over multiple column rows; abbeydale v308 combines a forge court, wheel and arcaded loft; hawthornloom v592 bridges two separate anchor rooms.

Concrete difference: one continuous building is banked at its rear, yet open at its lower front; the rear upper loading door and front lower arcade share a real floor section. It is not a wholly raised pavilion or a buried roof.

Reject if: the earth is an incidental mound touching an otherwise ordinary barn, the lower front becomes a painted arcade, the rear doorway is below/above its approach, or bank mass fills the front void. This is a higher-risk silhouette candidate: retain it only if official native views plainly show the two access levels.

Shape key: single-gabled-bank-barn-rear-earth-entry-at-upper-floor-exposed-deep-front-lower-arcade.

rows.design:
Use: a raised grain-store exhibit; no pest, harvest or storage economy.

Volume and roof: a low, broad, enclosed timber granary sits on several SHORT individually mushroom-capped stone supports. Each support has a narrower stone stem, a visibly wider cap and a real bearing relationship to the continuous timber floor. A continuous low air gap remains beneath the entire building, rather than a walkable open ground storey. One broad complete hipped slate/wood roof caps the squat body. A raised loading porch is actually recessed into one short end under that roof, not pasted onto a closed facade.

Entrance and openings: short steps reach the porch floor and its set-back double timber door. Sparse small high windows or vents protect the enclosed-store reading. The capped supports and recessed entry must be large enough for native viewing; avoid an arbitrary forest of tiny invisible legs.

Closest existing structures: burnham v324 stands on tall thin uncapped piles; faversham v276 has an occupied-height open columned market storey; hartcurrier v784 uses a continuous masonry spine; hawthornloom v592 uses separate occupied anchor rooms. Willington v196 is fully grounded masonry with stepped gables and a louvre turret. Also compare UKF021-S in british-use-scales-agriculture021.js: that earlier farmhouse/crop compound already includes a separate small raised gabled granary on four short UNCAPPED rectangular stone blocks, with side loading doors. Raised floor plus short stone supports alone is therefore not new.

Concrete difference: a squat closed granary supported across its whole floor by short separated capped stone staddles, with a low continuous ventilation gap and an elevated recessed loading bay. The combination of a substantial whole-store air gap, genuinely overhanging mushroom caps, broad hip, squat standalone mass and deep recessed END-loading porch must distinguish it from that small farm granary. Support height, shape, spacing, floor relationship and entry are the distinguishing architecture, not just timber colour.

Reject if: the gap fills in, the supports become tall generic piles, caps are only painted bands, or the result reads as a smaller Burnham lighthouse with its tower cut down. The roof stays broad and low; there is no lantern or lookout room.

Shape key: squat-enclosed-hipped-timber-granary-short-mushroom-stone-supports-continuous-low-air-gap-recessed-loading-porch.

rows.design:
Use: a covered pedestrian-bridge pavilion displayed as a landmark; no new functional path, road connection, water crossing or pedestrian routing.

Volume and roof: a short high enclosed timber bridge room on slender grounded piers is joined at both ends to substantial enclosed descending stair ranges. The stairs are real stepped geometry, not solid end houses. The entrance portals and upper landing openings must expose enough real treads/landings to establish the stair reading; opaque walls hiding every step would leave only source-level evidence. The inclined underside and open ground beneath must also remain visible. Each stair range has a roof that follows its descent, while the central level span has a complete gable. The overall side silhouette rises from both ends to a broad central crown and descends again. Keep the rise modest enough for two credible stair runs inside the existing 2×2 plot.

Entrance and openings: actual open ground-level entrance portals at both low ends, landings at the level span, and a sequence of long narrow side windows whose heads/sills track the stair ranges. Closed side walls follow the floor rise with genuine thickness; space below the high span and between supporting piers stays open. No stream, road repaint or external terrain is needed.

Closest existing structures: pulteney v252 is a level multi-arch masonry bridge carrying two shop rows; hawthornloom v592 is a level gambrel room on two solid anchor buildings; penguin v424 uses open interlaced cantilever spiral ramps; rillramblers v756 is an enclosed rising near-ring spiral. Also compare the older british-station-art008.js passage: it already has an elevated OPEN footbridge with real descending stairs. Catmint cannot claim bridge-plus-stairs alone as new; the closed inclined stair volumes, their descending roofs, exposed entrance/landing sightlines and whole standalone silhouette are the proposed distinction.

Concrete difference: two opposing roofed stair volumes are the primary end masses of one up-and-over enclosed route, connected by a short level covered span. Its circulation volume and roof section rise and descend linearly, without arch-shop rows, anchor houses, spiral loops or a ring.

Reject if: end stairs become ordinary rectangular buildings, the roof is one level plank across the whole asset, the support void is filled, or its identity depends on an added road/water texture. Both endpoint doors and both stair transitions must be visible in the four-view set.

Shape key: enclosed-up-and-over-footbridge-level-gabled-central-span-two-opposed-descending-roofed-stair-ranges-open-piers.

rows.design:
Use: a compact bell-practice room and architectural exhibit; bells, clocks and sounds are not new gameplay.

Volume and roof: one low, broad square masonry bellroom is dominated by a tall eight-faced broach spire that rises DIRECTLY from its square eaves. Four real triangular corner broach planes resolve square corners into the eight sloping roof faces. There is no intermediate octagonal room/drum, onion/ogee bulge, open lattice spire, stacked roof cap or tower-stage ladder. The spire is a substantial portion of the total mass, not a tiny topper on a familiar tower.

Entrance and openings: a single recessed ground door and two high paired louvred/round-headed acoustic openings on the exposed faces. Louvres should remain actual front/rear thickness where promised, without needing a miniature moving bell. Keep lower walls squat enough that the square-to-octagon transition is readable at native scale.

Closest existing structures: stalbans v240 is a tall four-stage square flint belfry with an actual battlemented flat top (its declared inventory text incorrectly says ogee); glasgow v388 carries an open pierced spire above a multi-stage tower/court compound; alaronde v160 starts from an already sixteen-sided house; briarwatch v596 has a hexagonal lookout with two-stage caps; willington v196 has stepped gables and a small louvre turret. The older flintParishChurch007 in british-publiclife-art.js has a tall three-stage square tower with an open recessed battlemented top, not a direct broach spire on a low room.

Concrete difference: a short square room and one dominant CLOSED faceted spire with explicit corner broaches, without an intervening polygonal storey. The square-to-eight transition and low-room/high-roof proportion must define the whole object, not merely a changed finial.

Reject if: it becomes a reduced St Albans with a renamed cap, the broaches are decorative triangles over an unchanged pyramid, an octagonal drum is inserted, or the spire is too small to distinguish from existing lanterns. A geometry check must prove the actual corner-to-eight-plane transition, followed by native visual review.

Shape key: low-square-masonry-bellroom-dominant-closed-eight-face-broach-spire-four-true-corner-transition-planes-no-drum.

rows.design:
Use: a ventilated timber-seasoning and pole-repair store, shown as architecture only. No drying, storage, crafting or resource-production simulation.

Volume and roof: a long two-storey rectangular building has solid masonry rear and end walls, but BOTH ground-level work bays and a deep upper gallery remain genuinely open across the long front. A substantial intermediate timber floor and several full-height braced front posts are exposed. One uninterrupted asymmetric single-pitch slate roof descends from the high rear wall to the lower front post line. This is not a closed upper house on columns: both levels are deep usable open-front spaces.

Entrance and openings: an exterior end stair reaches a real upper landing and side doorway into the open gallery. Ground bays are entered directly from the front. The back wall can have a few small high windows, but neither open tier is glazed. A low protective upper rail is permissible only if it leaves a large open area above and does not obscure the gallery depth. Keep the front bays broad, with a restrained number of substantial posts rather than a dense screen of hairline decoration.

Closest existing structures: elmstone v700 is one open cutting-shed level plus a rear tool strip; faversham v276 has an enclosed upper hall over an open columned ground floor; bishoplloyd v532 has one narrow first-floor gallery between a solid ground shop and several enclosed upper floors. Chatham v288 is a long enclosed three-storey ropery, not two deep open tiers.

Concrete difference: two stacked full-depth open work floors beneath one monopitch roof, with a visible intermediate floor, solid back/end enclosure and exterior upper-level access. Unlike the proposed bank barn, neither floor is a closed upper granary, no earth bank provides access, and the main roof is a single plane rather than a complete gable.

Reject if: either tier is filled with a dark painted panel; the upper opening is merely a shallow decorative balcony; the intermediate floor disappears behind posts; or a gable/hip and enclosed upper walls reduce it to Faversham or Elmstone. Two open tiers must be visually clear from the actual front-oblique native views, with the solid back and sloping roof legible in rear views.

Shape key: long-two-tier-deep-open-front-seasoning-loft-solid-masonry-back-and-ends-real-middle-floor-single-monopitch-end-stair.
